ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 6 — Sick Visit — Elisabeth of Austria — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for vomiting and diarrhea

text.paragraph: Vomiting and diarrhea for two days. [S]

Empress Elisabeth asked for a same-day visit. Two days ago, the day after one of her travelling party fell ill with the same thing, she began vomiting, about four times that day, followed by watery diarrhea five or six times a day. The vomiting stopped yesterday evening; she has kept down sips of water and tea since, but almost no food, and has had diarrhea three times today. No blood in the stool, no severe abdominal pain. She feels light-headed when she stands and her mouth is dry. She takes sertraline 50 mg daily and vitamin D, and has taken both. She was frightened that her team would think she had made herself sick; she has not, and she has not used laxatives or diuretics. She leaves to travel again in three days. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1894-05-26; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Tired but alert; temperature 37.6 C; weight 51.0 kg, down 1 kg in a month with the illness
Seated blood pressure 96/60, pulse 74; standing after two minutes 84/56, pulse 96, with light-headedness; regular rhythm
Dry mucous membranes; no parotid swelling or dental erosion
Soft, mildly tender all over, no guarding; active bowel sounds

Weight loss to a body mass index of 16.0 (47.4 kg at 172 cm), about 6 kg over six months, with fatigue, swelling of both ankles, dizziness on standing, slow pulse and cold intolerance; cause not established at intake; a restrictive eating disorder suspected, with thyroid disease, celiac disease, diabetes, malignancy and adrenal insufficiency to be excluded; eating disorders psychiatry consultation requested
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented restrictive eating, low weight and swelling; superseded by the diagnosis at the consultation.

Anorexia nervosa, restricting type, moderate (DSM-5-TR), with compulsive exercise and frequent self-weighing, beginning in early adulthood; complicated at diagnosis by sinus bradycardia, orthostatic dizziness, ankle edema, mild anemia and leukopenia, low glucose, raised ALT and low phosphate after refeeding began
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, linked to her documented restrictive eating and exercise and to the retrospective diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (R).
Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate, with persistent grief for her son, who died five years ago; passive thoughts of death without intent or plan at intake
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented mourning and ever-deepening depressions; not a claim that she was so diagnosed.

Acute viral gastroenteritis, caught from a member of her travelling party, with mild dehydration, orthostatic hypotension and mild hypokalemia; no purging behavior; managed with oral rehydration and potassium; resolved
S — Synthetic acute problem; not a historical claim.

Low bone mass (osteopenia) of the lumbar spine and hip after decades of low weight: lumbar spine T-score -2.1, femoral neck T-score -1.8; FRAX 10-year probabilities 6.8% for a major osteoporotic fracture and 1.2% for hip fracture; no fractures
S — Synthetic modern finding on DXA; not a historical claim.

list.item:
Acute viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration and hypokalemia (A08.4). A contact with the same illness, vomiting that has stopped and watery diarrhea without blood fit a viral gastroenteritis. She is mildly dehydrated with orthostatic hypotension, but drinking. Potassium 3.3 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 0.78 mg/dL, glucose 72 mg/dL, magnesium 1.7 mg/dL. The ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 452 ms. In anorexia nervosa, low potassium and a low glucose reserve make this riskier than usual, and sertraline adds a little to QT risk, so ondansetron is not used; the vomiting has stopped and an antiemetic is not needed. Stool tests and antibiotics are not indicated for a short watery illness without blood or high fever under the IDSA guideline. Her account, the absence of knuckle calluses, parotid swelling and dental erosion, and the illness in her contact do not suggest purging. [S]
Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent amounts, aiming for about 2 to 2.5 liters a day while the diarrhea lasts.
Potassium chloride 20 mEq daily for three days.
Back to the meal plan in steps over two to three days, with the dietitian by telephone tomorrow; no make-up restriction afterwards.
Continue sertraline.
Repeat electrolytes and magnesium in two to three days, before she travels.
Go to an emergency department for inability to keep fluids down, fainting, palpitations, blood in the stool or confusion.

Anorexia nervosa, restricting type (F50.011). The illness has cost about a kilogram; the team plan continues. [S]
Weight check at the next review.

Clin Infect Dis 2017;65(12):e45-e80) (2017)

Follow-up: Electrolytes in two to three days. Telephone check tomorrow. Twenty-one-week review as booked. Next scheduled visit 1894-06-30: twenty-one-week review: weight, mood, the gastroenteritis, and care while travelling. [S]
